title: U.S. House · New York's 10th Congressional District
area: Parts of Lower Manhattan and Brooklyn, including Park Slope, Sunset Park, Borough Park, Bay Ridge, and Lower Manhattan neighborhoods such as Tribeca and the Financial District.

context.text: Brad Lander defeated incumbent Rep. Daniel Goldman in the June 23, 2026 Democratic primary, 66.0% to 33.8% (58,047 to 29,781 votes). Because Goldman lost the primary, he is not on the November 3 general-election ballot.

Jennifer Moore advanced as the Republican and Conservative Party nominee after both parties' primaries were canceled (she was unopposed). Brad Lander advanced as the Working Families Party nominee after that primary was also canceled.

Nickie Kane ran in the Democratic primary and lost; Ballotpedia lists her as a write-in candidate on the "No Kings Party" line in the general election. Her campaign site instructs supporters to write in her name if it does not appear printed on the ballot.

candidates.name: Brad Lander
candidates.ballotNote: Won the June 23 Democratic primary, defeating incumbent Rep. Daniel Goldman

summary.text: Brad Lander is the Democratic nominee for NY-10 and a former New York City Comptroller (2022-2026). A Brooklyn community-development leader before entering government, he served on the New York City Council from 2010 to 2021, ran for mayor in 2025, and defeated incumbent Rep. Daniel Goldman in the June 23, 2026 Democratic primary. Reports list endorsements from Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Sen. Bernie Sanders, and Sen. Elizabeth Warren; his campaign website says he is running to "fight, not fold" against the Trump administration and for an affordable New York.

background.text: Born July 8, 1969, and raised in Creve Coeur, a suburb of St. Louis, Missouri; graduated from Parkway North High School in 1987.
Graduated from the University of Chicago (bachelor's degree, 1991) and holds master's degrees in social anthropology from University College London and in city planning from the Pratt Institute.

Before elected office, directed the nonprofits Fifth Avenue Committee (1993-2003) and the Pratt Center for Community Development (2003-2009). According to his campaign website, the groups built and preserved affordable housing and ran job-training programs.

Served on the New York City Council representing District 39 in Brooklyn (including Park Slope and Kensington) from 2010 to 2021, when term limits ended his tenure; he co-founded the Council's Progressive Caucus. His campaign website cites among his Council achievements the Gowanus rezoning, scheduling and delivery-worker pay laws, and the Independent Expenditure Disclosure Act.

Elected New York City Comptroller in 2021 and served from January 1, 2022 to January 1, 2026, as the city's chief financial and accountability officer overseeing its pension funds; he did not seek re-election as comptroller in 2025.
Announced in July 2024 that he would run for mayor in the 2025 Democratic primary; on June 13, 2025 he and Zohran Mamdani cross-endorsed each other, and Mamdani went on to win the primary.
According to his campaign website, he was handcuffed and detained by federal agents at 26 Federal Plaza in Manhattan in June 2025 while escorting an asylum seeker out of immigration court.

Announced his candidacy for NY-10 on December 10, 2025, and defeated incumbent Rep. Daniel Goldman in the June 23, 2026 Democratic primary, 66.0% to 33.8%; he also appears on the Working Families Party line.
Lives in Brooklyn with his wife, Meg Barnette; they raised two children, according to his campaign website.

priorities.text: Named housing, healthcare, and protecting immigrants as his top priorities for the general election, saying of Republican health policy: "Last year, Republicans voted to double people's premiums on the exchanges, to rip healthcare away from people, to cut Medicare and Medicaid."

Says Democrats should refuse to support any budget that does not restore expired ACA premium subsidies: "When we win back the House...we're going to run that fight again. And we'll only vote for a budget that restores those healthcare subsidies, so people can afford their lives better."

Says voters are frustrated with politicians who take corporate PAC money and look like they are doing the work of Wall Street, crypto, and AIPAC, and his campaign says it is fighting to get that kind of money out of politics.

positions.summary: Supports restoring expired ACA premium subsidies and opposes Republican efforts to cut Medicare and Medicaid.
positions.quote: Last year, Republicans voted to double people's premiums on the exchanges, to rip healthcare away from people, to cut Medicare and Medicaid.

positions.summary: Campaign platform calls for taxing wealthy individuals and billionaires more aggressively.
Campaign platform calls for increasing apartment construction along with housing vouchers to address affordability.
Campaign describes opposition to federal immigration enforcement actions, framing them as targeting immigrant neighbors.
As a City Council member, voted yes on the Climate Mobilization Act (Local Law 97), which set greenhouse-gas emissions limits for large buildings.
As a City Council member, voted yes on the bill setting a minimum per-trip payment rate for app-based food delivery workers.

record.text: As NYC Comptroller, released an audit (published November 20, 2024) finding NYCHA paid vendors $135.6 million in smaller purchases (under $50,000, including routine repairs and maintenance) during 2022 and 2023 with far less oversight than larger contracts, and that 46% of the value of purchase orders examined ($301,678 of $648,786) lacked evidence the work was performed; called for a new vendor scorecard based on real-time resident feedback.
Sponsored Int. No. 1017-C, the Freelance Isn't Free Act, requiring written contracts and timely payment for freelance workers; passed the City Council 51-0 on October 27, 2016.
Voted yes on Int. No. 1253-C, the Climate Mobilization Act (Local Law 97 of 2019), setting greenhouse-gas emissions limits for large buildings, which passed the City Council 45-2 on April 18, 2019.

Voted yes on Int. No. 2294-A, establishing minimum per-trip payments for third-party food-delivery and courier-service workers, which passed the City Council 40-3 (as part of a coupled vote with related bills) on September 23, 2021.

As a City Council member, was the lead sponsor of New York City's plastic bag fee/ban and Styrofoam ban bills, and was an early sponsor of the Council's waste equity and commercial waste zone legislation.
According to his campaign biography, delivered job protections for freelancers and fast-food workers and a $15 minimum wage for delivery workers and Uber drivers as a City Council member.
Co-founded the New York City Council's Progressive Caucus during his time on the Council.

candidates.name: Jennifer Moore
candidates.ballotNote: Advanced as the Republican and Conservative Party nominee after both primaries were canceled (unopposed)

summary.text: Jennifer Moore is the Republican and Conservative Party nominee for NY-10. The New York Post describes her as a Brooklyn GOP operative; she said she is running to give voters a choice after Brad Lander defeated incumbent Rep. Daniel Goldman in the June 23 Democratic primary.

background.text: Described by the New York Post as a Brooklyn Republican Party operative; she advanced as the Republican and Conservative Party candidate after both June 23, 2026 primaries were canceled.

priorities.text: Says Lander's primary win against Goldman has drawn new interest to the race and that she aims to bring in support from voters across party lines who oppose Lander's ideology.
priorities.quote: The political earthquake last night of Brad Lander unseating an incumbent has infused interest in this race and my goal is to seize this opportunity and engage more support from voters registered to all parties who oppose Lander's radical ideology.

candidates.name: Nickie Kane
candidates.ballotNote: Ran in and lost the Democratic primary; listed by Ballotpedia as a write-in candidate on the "No Kings Party" line for the general election

summary.text: Nickie Kane is a community advocate and grassroots organizer campaigning as a write-in candidate on the No Kings Party line in the NY-10 general election. According to her campaign website, she is a lifelong New Yorker who worked in retail, banking, advertising and human resources and previously ran for New York City Council in District 39. Ballotpedia lists her among Democratic primary candidates who withdrew or were disqualified.

background.text: Describes herself as a lifelong New Yorker who began working after high school, first in retail and then in banking at Amalgamated Bank, North Fork Bank and Capital One.

Says she later worked in advertising at Publicis Groupe, earned a degree in new media from Queensborough Community College and a degree in psychology from The City College of New York, and worked in human resources at Disney ABC Television Group and in small business lending.
Says she is studying to become a paralegal at New York City College of Technology and previously ran for New York City Council in District 39.

Sought the Democratic nomination in NY-10 but is listed by Ballotpedia among candidates who withdrew or were disqualified before the June 23, 2026 primary; her campaign website describes legal challenges she brought over ballot access. She now describes herself as a write-in candidate on the No Kings Party line.
Describes her campaign as "people-powered" and herself as a community advocate and grassroots organizer; her campaign site says she also started the Independent Voters Alliance in June 2025.

priorities.text: Supports closing tax loopholes and raising the effective tax rate on the highest wealth brackets to fund childcare, healthcare, housing, and transportation for working families.
Supports Medicare for All along with full funding for mental health care, community clinics, reproductive care, and gender-affirming care.
priorities.quote: Healthcare is a right. I support Medicare for All, full funding for mental health care, community clinics, reproductive care, and gender-affirming care so every person in NY-10 gets the care they need without debt.

priorities.text: Supports strong tenant protections, rent stabilization, and investment in permanently affordable, community-controlled housing.

positions.summary: Supports Medicare for All and full public funding for mental health care, community clinics, reproductive care, and gender-affirming care.
positions.quote: Healthcare is a right. I support Medicare for All, full funding for mental health care, community clinics, reproductive care, and gender-affirming care so every person in NY-10 gets the care they need without debt.

positions.summary: Supports strong tenant protections and rent stabilization, and opposes displacement from gentrification.
Supports closing tax loopholes and raising the effective tax rate on the highest wealth brackets to fund childcare, healthcare, housing, and transportation.
Supports a Green New Deal-style program creating union jobs, investing in clean energy, upgrading public housing, and protecting frontline communities from flooding and heat.

Opposes further U.S. offensive military aid to Israel and supports the Block the Bombs Act, while backing conditioned defensive aid such as Iron Dome funding tied to de-escalation and halting West Bank settlement expansion.
Opposes increased police funding in favor of community-based violence prevention and mental health crisis response teams, saying public safety comes from "stability and care."

researchNotes: Jennifer Moore has published no detailed federal policy platform and has not completed Ballotpedia's Candidate Connection survey; her record above reflects the limited public statements available. Brad Lander has no documented federal legislative record (never having served in Congress); his record section covers his City Council and Comptroller record, including three City Council floor votes verified against the official Stated Meeting minutes on legistar.council.nyc.gov. Per the research brief, Lander's and any incumbent's future FEC finance totals and federal floor votes are added separately by script. Jennifer Moore: no campaign website, questionnaire or issue statements were found in searches; only her June 2026 statement to the New York Post is documented, so no positions were added. Jennifer Moore's biography is limited to ballot status and one news description; no campaign biography page was found.
